citations.desc: Attending veterinarian and adequate veterinary care (dealers and exhibitors).
citations.narrative:
The facility failed to effectively observe animals to assess their health and well-being and convey timely and accurate
information on problems of animal health, behavior and well-being to the attending veterinarian for the following animals:
USDA inspectors observed an adult Many-Banded Aracari, named “Dewey,” that was unable to consistently perch on an
appropriately sized perch. About every 10-15 seconds, the animal slipped and was unable to firmly grip the perch. When
asked if the veterinarian had seen the animal for this concern, the facility representative indicated that it had not and that
facility staff had not observed the issue.
Keepers observed an adult Bearded Saki named “Half-Beard” (22M007) to have a new injury to its left hand on June 4,
2026. Daily observation notes from that day indicate “Half-Beard’s finger remains slightly swollen. The bone remains
exposed and white.” The animal has a history of self-inflicted behaviors with its most recent injury to the tail on April 2,
2026. A medical entry dated March 11, 2026, documents that this individual has already self-amputated a portion of its
right third digit. Despite this, the facility did not report the animal’s condition to the attending veterinarian.
Failure to timely and accurately communicate problems of animal health to the attending veterinarian can result in longer
durations of pain and distress, and a worse prognosis.
Ensure there is direct and frequent communication to the attending veterinarian.
Correct by August 5, 2026.

The facility housed a rabbit with two adult Burrowing Owls in the same enclosure. While the enclosure provided sufficient
space, shelter, and access to food and water, rabbits are a species that are not permitted to be co-housed with any other
species, unless for specific scientific purposes. Housing rabbits with other species may result in injury or compatibility
issues. Correct by ensuring rabbits are not housed in the same primary enclosure with any other species of animals.
Correct by August 5, 2026.

An outdoor enclosure housing pygmy marmosets does not provide protection from the sun. The enclosure has clear
plastic corrugated roofing for protection from inclement weather but does not provide adequate shade.
Failure to provide adequate shade exposes the animals to direct sunlight for extended periods, increasing their risk of
heat stress and discomfort.
Correct by ensuring nonhuman primates in outdoor housing facilities are always provided adequate shelter from the
elements, including direct sunlight. The housing must provide protection from the sun, rain, snow, wind, and cold, and
from any weather conditions that may occur.
Correct by August 5, 2026.

The facility’s current program for the control of insects is ineffective. Multiple live cockroaches were observed in and
around the enclosures for the giant anteaters in the “Bridge” section of the facility. The walkways in front of the enclosures
contained multiple dead cockroaches. The facility confirmed they currently spray for cockroaches; however, the presence
of live cockroaches indicates that the program is ineffective.
Pests such as cockroaches can adversely affect the health and well-being of the animals by spreading disease and
contaminating food, surfaces and animal housing areas.
A safe and effective program for the control of insects, ectoparasites, and avian and mammalian pests shall be
established and maintained.
Correct by August 18, 2026.

The housing facilities for various avian species are not being kept in good repair.
Numerous metal beams that comprise the enclosures throughout Aviary 1901 were severely rusted. The rust covered
large portions of the beams, and was dark reddish-brown to nearly black, indicating more than surface rust. The beams
had a rough, crust-like build up where the metal surfaces have deteriorated. An enclosure in Aviary 1901 containing one
adult Curl-Crested Aracari had a broken lock on its door. There was no additional method to secure the bird inside the
enclosure. An enclosure housing one toucan above the female giant anteater had a hole in the metal wiring approximately
2 inches by 2 inches in size; the exposed ends of the wiring created sharp points. Multiple bird cages throughout Aviary
1901 had broken sections of wiring that created sharp points.
Housing facilities with sharp points created by poorly maintained wire pose a risk of injury to the birds housing in them.
Correct by ensuring that bird enclosures are maintained in good repair, protect the birds from injury and restrict other
animals from entering.
Correct by September 30, 2026.

The “Bridge” area primary enclosures that house several adult Black Mandible Toucans do not provide protection from the
sun. The enclosure has clear plastic corrugated roofing for protection from inclement weather but doesn’t provide any
shade from direct sunlight.
Failure to provide adequate shade exposes the animals to direct sunlight for extended periods, increasing their risk of
heat stress and discomfort.
Shelter must be adequate to protect the birds from any adverse weather conditions and constructed to provide sufficient
space to comfortably hold all of the birds at the same time. Outdoor housing facilities must provide adequate shelter
appropriate to the species to allow the birds to access protection from direct sunlight in order to ensure their welfare.
Correct by August 5, 2026.

An outdoor enclosure containing two adult Wattled Guans provided perches that were not appropriate for this species.
The perches consisted of 2x4 wood boards mounted so that the 2-in side was vertically situated. Improper perch size,
shape, and texture can lead to health issues like pododermatitis and put strain on the bird’s feet and legs. If the enclosure
houses birds that rest by perching, there must be perches available that are appropriate to the age and species of the
birds housed therein and a sufficient number of perches of appropriate size, shape, strength, texture and placement to
comfortably hold all the birds in the primary enclosure at the same time, including birds that are ranked low in a
dominance hierarchy.
Correct by August 5, 2026.

citations.desc: Environment enhancement to promote psychological well-being.
citations.narrative:
The facility does not have an environmental enhancement plan (EEP) approved by the current attending veterinarian. The
current attending veterinarian started on July 20, 2026, the day of the inspection and has not approved the environmental
enhancement plan. Many enclosures were bare with only perches and their food receptacles present. Failure to
implement and follow an EEP as outlined can negatively impact the health and well-being of the animals. Exhibitors must
develop, document, and follow a species-appropriate plan for environmental enhancement that is approved by the
attending veterinarian to adequately promote the psychological well-being of birds.
Correct by August 5, 2026.

Inspectors identified expired supplements in the bird nursery area. A Probios supplement expired April 25, 2025, a vitamin
mix without an expiration date, and Auklet vitamin expired April 2025.
Feeding expired supplements to birds can compromise their health by provided degraded nutrients, which may result in
reduced effectiveness.
The food must be wholesome, palatable to the birds, and free of contamination.
Correct by August 10, 2026.

Food receptacles in the jungle area holding ½ cut papayas were severely rusted with deep fissures and swollen areas
that make the surface unable to be sanitized.
Failure to appropriately maintain clean food receptacles promotes unsanitary surfaces that can harm the birds’ health
upon ingestion of contaminated food.
Food receptacles must be kept clean and sanitized.
Correct by August 10, 2026.

citations.desc: Cleaning, sanitization, housekeeping, and pest control.
citations.narrative:
The facility is not removing excreta and food waste from the primary enclosure as often as necessary to prevent
excessive accumulation of feces and food waste. USDA inspectors observed old food accumulated (over a dozen pieces
of desiccated rabbit remains) in and around the Harpy Eagle enclosure in the netting above Aviary 1901.
Failure to regularly remove excreta and food waste creates unsanitary conditions that can be detrimental to avian health
by increasing the risk of disease and attracting pests.
Excreta and food waste must be removed from the primary enclosures and from under and around primary enclosures as
often as necessary to prevent excessive accumulation of feces and food waste, to prevent soiling of the birds contained in
the primary enclosure, and to reduce disease hazards, insects, pests, and odors.
Correct by August 5, 2026.

citations.desc: Cleaning, sanitization, housekeeping, and pest control.
citations.narrative:
The facility’s current program for the control of insect and mammalian pests is ineffective. Aviary 1901 has multiple
enclosures housing various species of birds that show signs of heavy ant activity. Extensive amounts of ants were present
in the fresh food, on food receptacles and throughout enclosures for a vast majority of the outdoor bird enclosures. Live
cockroaches were seen on the walls and within the enclosures of the birds housed in the Bridge area. Although the facility
sprays, the current program is not effective as evidenced by the findings above.
Pests such as rodents, cockroaches and ants can adversely affect the health and well-being of the birds by spreading
disease and contaminating food, surfaces and animal housing areas.
A safe and effective program for the control of insects, ectoparasites, and avian and mammalian pests shall be
established and maintained.
Correct by August 18, 2026.
This inspection and exit interview were conducted with the facility representative.
You may appeal all or part of any inspection report by submitting a written statement contesting the findings—along with
any supporting documentation—to the Deputy Administrator. Appeals of routine, focused, or attempted inspections must
be received within 21 days of report issuance as shown by the signature line of this report.
Appeals may be sent by email to AnimalCare@usda.gov.
